summary: Defines a certificate extension that states which Attribute Certificate Policies apply to a given attribute certificate. A relying party can then check whether to accept the attributes based on specific policies. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A badge that says which rulebook it follows, so whoever checks it can decide if they trust the rulebook behind it.

questions: what is an attribute certificate policy
what is the ac policies extension
what happens if an ac has no matching policy
subtitle: A certificate extension that says which policies an attribute certificate was issued under.

tldr.problem: A relying party validating an Attribute Certificate (AC) has no explicit way to tell which policies govern how it was generated, issued and revoked.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4476 defines the AC policies extension, a list of policy object identifiers (OIDs), each optionally with a pointer to a practice statement or a user notice.
tldr.outcome: A relying party can reject an AC whose listed policies do not fit its purpose. The RFC defines no policies themselves.

facts.label: Qualifier types
facts.value: ACPS pointer and AC user notice

today: RFC 4476 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why AC Policies Need Naming
sections.content:
When a Certificate Authority issues a Public Key Certificate, it can perform various levels of verification of the subject identity. It makes its verification procedures and other operational rules visible through a certificate policy, which a certificate policies extension can reference.

This document does the same for Attribute Certificates (defined in RFC 3281). It defines an extension that explicitly states which AC policies apply to a given AC, but not the policies themselves. The goal is to give relying parties an additional test when validating an AC.
sections.eli5: A school ID shows which school issued it. This extension is a line on the badge saying which set of rules the badge was handed out under.

sections.title: What an AC Policy Is
sections.content:
An Attribute Certificate Policy (ACP) is a named set of rules that indicates the applicability of an AC to a particular community and/or class of applications with common security requirements. It defines rules for generating, issuing and revoking ACs, and may include rules for attribute registration.

An Attribute Authority (AA) does not necessarily support only one ACP. For each AC it delivers, though, the AA SHALL make sure the policy applies to all the attributes in it. Policies may be defined by any organization with a need, and their object identifiers are assigned under X.660 and ISO 9834-1. The scope of the RFC excludes the detailed content of ACPs.
sections.eli5: A policy is a rulebook for handing out badges. Anyone who needs one can write their own and give it a number.

sections.title: Extension Syntax
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-acPolicies, which is arc 15 under id-pe. Its value, AcPoliciesSyntax, is a sequence of one or more PolicyInformation entries. Each has a policyIdentifier (an OID) and optionally a sequence of policy qualifiers.

Two qualifier types are supported. The ACPS pointer (id-qt-acps) holds a URI pointing to an Attribute Certification Practice Statement published by the AA; how it is processed is a local matter. The AC user notice (id-qt-acunotice) is meant for display to a relying party and has two optional fields, noticeRef and explicitText. The explicit text has a maximum size of 200 characters. If both are present and the notice text can be located, that text SHOULD be displayed, otherwise the explicit text SHOULD be.

To promote interoperability the RFC RECOMMENDS that policy information consist of only an OID. If several policies are listed their requirements must not conflict; one may refine another.
sections.eli5: The badge has a list of rulebook numbers. It can also carry a web address for the full rules and a short note for people to read.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Process It
sections.content:
The AA may mark the extension critical or non-critical. An application that recognizes the extension SHALL process it regardless of the criticality flag. If it is non-critical and not recognized, the application MAY ignore it.

If the extension is critical or recognized, the attributes SHALL only be used for the purpose and under the rules of one of the listed policies. The application MUST use the list to decide whether using the attributes for a transaction is appropriate. If none of the listed policies is adequate, the AC MUST be rejected.
sections.eli5: If the checker knows about the rulebook list, they must look at it. If none of the listed rulebooks suits their job, they say no.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The ACP applies to all attributes in one AC, and since an AC may be issued under more than one ACP, its attributes MUST comply with all of them. A relying party MUST determine that the AC was issued by a trusted AA and then that it has the appropriate policy.

The RFC also warns about AA private key compromise or loss, the freshness of revocation status, weak key lengths or hash algorithms, and a rogue CA that reuses an issuer name when an AC is tied to a certificate through baseCertificateID. Implementers MUST ensure only attributes the issuer is trusted to issue are used in authorization decisions.

For IANA, the OID was assigned from an arc delegated to the PKIX Working Group, and no further action is needed.
sections.eli5: A badge is only as good as the people who print it and keep their stamp safe. Check the printer is trusted and only believe what that printer is allowed to say.
